question: For a simple undirected graph with N vertices given by its adjacency matrix A: (1) what does the entry (A^k)_{ij} represent, (2) how can one determine from A whether the graph is connected, and (3) what is the definition of a path between vertices n_i and n_j?

sources.title: Graph Theory (Գրաֆների տեսություն), study manual
sources.notes: Local file at repository root, not under sources/. Printed pages are PDF pages minus one; cited by printed page. Pages viewed as images: printed 11, 16, 21, 22, 23, 48, 49. Armenian quotes were transcribed from the page images (subscripts flattened, for example u0 for u with subscript 0). Textbook for a university course; primary for definitions and numbering. A text-layer search of all 216 PDF pages for the adjacency-matrix term hit printed pp. 7, 11, 12, 34, 61 only; only p. 11 was viewed; the others are as recorded in graph-sources.md and were not re-viewed in this run. The book has no walk-counting theorem and no matrix connectivity test, as far as that search shows.

sources.notes: Read pages 1-2. Theorem 2 is stated correctly but its proof is only a sketch, and sentence 4 of the sketch says (I + A)^(n-1) aggregates all paths of length at most n-1, which is incorrect for paths (it aggregates walks). No sum form A + ... + A^(n-1) appears in these notes.

claims.text: For a simple graph with adjacency matrix A and a positive integer k, (A^k)_{ij} is the number of walks of length k from v_i to v_j (proved by induction on k).

support.quote: Let k be a positive integer. Then the entry in the (i, j)-position of the matrix A^k is the number of walks of length k from v_i to v_j in G.
For any j, k ∈ [n] and ℓ ∈ N, there are A^ℓ_jk walks of length ℓ from j to k.
Then for any two vertices i and j, the entry (A^k)_ij counts the number of walks of length k from vertex i to vertex j.

claims.text: The entry (A^k)_{ij} counts walks, not paths: matrix multiplication does not remember visited vertices.

support.quote: counts walks — not paths. This is because matrix multiplication accumulates all sequences of edges between two vertices, including those that revisit vertices and edges.

claims.text: (A^2)_{ii} equals the degree of n_i, so it is positive for any non-isolated vertex although no path of length 2 starts and ends at n_i. On the board graph (edges n1n2, n2n3) (A^2)_11 = 1 and (A^2)_22 = 2. Proved by module m1 as M1-2.

support.quote: The number of walks of length 2 from a vertex to itself is just the number of edges at that vertex, or the vertex degree.

claims.text: Paramadevan and Sotheeswaran Theorem 1 says the (i,j) entry of A^l is the number of different paths of length l between vertices i and j. The source never defines path. Under the walk reading, which its own proof and property 7 use, the sentence agrees with walk counting. Under the standard no-repeated-vertex meaning it is false: on the board graph (A^2)_11 = 1 with no path of length 2 from n1 to itself, and (A^3)_12 = 2 while only one path joins n1 to n2.

support.quote: the number of different paths of length l between the ith and j th vertices of G is equal to the (i, j)th entry of A^l_G.

claims.text: The same paper's property 7 states that the (i,j) entry of A^m counts walks of length m, so the paper is inconsistent with itself.

support.quote: The (i, j)th entry of A^m_G is equal to the number of walks of length m from vi to vj

claims.text: Paramadevan's proof of Theorem 2 says b_ij is the number of different paths of length less than n from i to j. Restated, B = A + A^2 has B_22 = 2 on the board graph while at most one path of length less than 3 joins n2 to itself, so the restated sentence is false.

support.quote: bij = number of different paths of length less than n from the vertex i to j.

claims.text: Bai's proof sketch says (I + A)^(n-1) aggregates all paths of length at most n-1. Restated, R = (I + A)^2 has R_11 = 2 on the board graph but only one path of length at most 2 joins n1 to itself (length 0); the matrix counts walks.

support.quote: (I + A)^(n−1) aggregates all paths of length ≤ n − 1.

contradictions.summary: Paramadevan Theorem 1 says the entry of A^l counts paths; Galway Theorem 1.1.3, Gotti Proposition 2 and Bai Theorem 1 say it counts walks. Walks hold: (A^2)_11 = 1 on the board graph with no path of length 2.
contradictions.resolution: Paper proves the walk statement and refutes the path restatement in one discussion item with the board counterexample.

contradictions.summary: Paramadevan Theorem 1 says paths; the same paper's property 7 says walks, both on p. 16.
contradictions.resolution: Cite the paper only for the statement of the test; note the internal inconsistency in the discussion.

contradictions.summary: Paramadevan's proof counts paths of length 1 to n-1 and sums them; the correct count is of walks, and the step from a nonzero entry to a path needs the walk-to-path result (Grinberg Corollary 2.9.7). The sum statement holds for off-diagonal entries only when read as walks.
contradictions.resolution: Paper proves the sum form itself using walk counting and the walk-to-path lemma.

contradictions.summary: Bai's sketch says (I + A)^(n-1) aggregates paths; Gotti's proof gets the same test through walks, the path bound, and the binomial identity. The test itself agrees in both; only the sketch sentence is wrong.
contradictions.resolution: Paper states the test, proves it via walks, and discusses the sketch sentence with a counterexample.

contradictions.summary: The textbook's path means no repeated edge (English trail) and its simple path means no repeated vertex; Grinberg and English usage call the latter path. The course convention follows the textbook's simple path.
contradictions.resolution: One three-column naming table; the paper writes simple path or course path and keeps the textbook's number beside each word.

contradictions.summary: Textbook Lemma 1.2.1 covers u different from v with no length bound; Grinberg Corollary 2.9.7 covers u = v and gives the bound k.
contradictions.resolution: Paper cites Lemma 1.2.1 for the course statement and Corollary 2.9.7 for the extended one, and proves the bound it uses.
